events.feedback:
Here is the evaluation for the Fiji Fan Palm (Pritchardia pacifica) data payload, focusing on content integrity, structural gaps, and multi-channel readiness.

Strengths
Canoe Plant & Cultural Narrative: Excellent historical framing—explaining how ancient Polynesian voyagers transported the seeds across open oceans and detailing the royal ai viu ceremonial fan/umbrella usage makes the content engaging.

In-Field Key Diagnostic: The comparison with Thurston’s Fan Palm (Pritchardia thurstonii) is outstanding. Highlighting that flower clusters stay tucked inside the crown (vs. arching outward 2 meters on P. thurstonii) gives visitors and staff a definitive visual diagnostic.

Lethal Yellowing Context: Accurately highlights high susceptibility to phytoplasma spread by the planthopper (Haxius crudus / Myndus crudus), providing essential disease risk context for Florida growers.

events.feedback:
What Still Needs Work (My Objections)

The Lethal Yellowing Stash: Burying Lethal Yellowing down in Notes is a missed opportunity. Pritchardia pacifica is one of the most susceptible palms in Florida, and Bradenton is right in the historical vector path. Move that threat up to More Information or frame it directly in Quick Hits: “Why is this tree rare in Gulf Coast gardens? It’s a sitting duck for Lethal Yellowing phytoplasma, meaning standing specimens in Manatee County are either lucky or heavily managed.”

Redundant Comparative Tangent: The More Information section still spends two entire bullet points comparing P. pacifica to Pritchardia thurstonii (flower stalk length, leaf ribs). Unless Palma Sola has a P. thurstonii planted right next to it, this is textbook fluff that bogs down a visitor standing in the heat. Cut it down to a single half-sentence or drop it completely to keep the text punchy.

events.feedback:
Yes. And I'm going to be considerably tougher on this one than the Majesty Palm, because there is a genuinely excellent story here, but I think you've mixed it with some claims that are too confident and some material that reads more like an internal horticulture memo than a botanical-garden page.
If I were a palm specialist visiting Palma Sola and scanning this QR code, my reaction would be:
“This is potentially a really interesting palm page. Whoever wrote it has found several things most garden labels completely miss. But I don't yet trust every sentence, and I think the writer is sometimes trying too hard to make the palm interesting.”
There are three genuinely strong stories here:
Its Pacific human history and dispersal.
Its unusual, almost undivided fan leaves.
Its vulnerability to lethal yellowing in Florida.
The first two could make a great visitor page. The third is important locally, but you're giving it way too much real estate.
